newsitem.title: UK: Chilean pension funds poised to move abroad - report.
newsitem.headline: Chilean pension funds poised to move abroad - report.

text.p: Chile's 13 private pension funds, which manage some $28 billion in assets on behalf of 5.4 million contributors, are expected to invest more abroad in 1997 as domestic interest rates decline, a report by ING Barings said.

The Administradoras de Fondos de Pensiones (AFP), which are funded by compulsory contributions from all Chilean employees, are currently limited to a total nine percent holding of foreign assets, 4.5 percent in foreign equities.
But the ING Barings report said some institutional investors planned to move aggressively into foreign markets.

"The president of the Association of Mutual Funds estimates that within three years mutual funds will have invested approximately $500 million abroad, an amount that exceeds what they currently hold in equities locally," said analyst Pablo Salcedo.
AFP foreign investment increased 18 percent month-on-month in November, but still represents just 0.5 percent of AFP assets under management, the ING Barings report said.
Salcedo also sees increased holdings of Chilean domestic equities, despite a slight dip in exposure for November 1996, the latest month for which data is available.
The poor performance of the Chilean stock market sidelined many AFPs apart from some take-up of new issues and cheaper ADRs such as Chilgner, Endesa and Soquimich.
"We expect the AFPs will maintain this strategy of selective buying of inexpensive stocks with a very timid increase in the equity weighting as a percentage of total assets," Salcedo said.
"This is supported by the fact that in the past three months AFPs have invested over 50 percent of their total monthly inflows in equities," he added.

"It is still too early to talk about an aggressive change in asset allocation, which may not come before a change in monetary policy, but the figures do indicate a trend towards higher equity exposure."

Government rules require that AFPs hold no more than 37 percent of total fund assets in domestic equities. As a percentage of funds under management, equities declined in November to 27.7 percent, from 28.7 percent in October 1996.
But Salcedo said the dip was partly offset by one of the largest capital inflows into equities over the past 12 months of $94 million, compared with a 12-month average of $70 million.

The report said Chilean pension funds would also benefit from expected changes this year in the pension fund law bill, still pending in Congress, which aims to reduce AFPs operating costs by limiting the turnover of affiliates in the system.
Salcedo also said AFP direct investments abroad, particularly in Argentina, Peru and Colombia, "should start consolidating and showing positive results".

The Chilean pension fund system, which has been turned round in under 15 years from a weighty government burden to a broadly self-supporting scheme, is seen as a possible model for many other developing and developing countries stuggling with their pensions funding to follow.
